summary: Lercanidipine is a third-generation lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for essential hypertension. Given once daily 10-20 mg at least 15 minutes before food, it lowers blood pressure through gradual peripheral arterial vasodilation, giving a 24-hour effect with minimal reflex tachycardia despite a short plasma half-life because of slow channel membrane binding. The maximal effect develops over about 2 weeks. Common effects are peripheral (ankle) edema, flushing, headache, and palpitations. Bioavailability rises about 4-fold with food, so fasting administration is essential; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, ciclosporin, and grapefruit are contraindicated. It is approved in Europe/UK (EMA/SmPC, BNF) and is not FDA-approved.

moa: Lercanidipine is a lipophilic dihydropyridine that selectively inhibits the transmembrane influx of calcium through L-type (slow) calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and cardiac muscle. By reducing calcium entry it produces a direct relaxant effect on vascular smooth muscle, lowering total peripheral resistance and arterial blood pressure. Its high lipophilicity allows accumulation in cell membranes and a slow, gradual onset with a long duration of action, so the antihypertensive effect persists over 24 hours despite a relatively short plasma half-life, with little reflex increase in heart rate. It has high vascular selectivity and negligible negative inotropic effect at therapeutic doses.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to lercanidipine, other dihydropyridines, or any excipient
Within one month of a myocardial infarction
Severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min), including dialysis patients
Concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin, troleandomycin)
Pregnancy and women of childbearing potential not using effective contraception
relative: Sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker
Mild to moderate hepatic or renal impairment (caution, slow titration)

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy. There are no adequate data on use in pregnant women, and other dihydropyridines have shown teratogenicity in animals. It must not be used during pregnancy or in women of childbearing potential unless effective contraception is used.
lact: Contraindicated during breastfeeding. It is not known whether lercanidipine is excreted in human milk; because of its lipophilicity excretion is likely, so breastfeeding should be avoided during treatment.
renal: Use with caution in mild to moderate renal impairment; the standard 10 mg dose may be used but increase to 20 mg with particular care. Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min) and in patients on dialysis.
hepatic: The antihypertensive effect may be enhanced in hepatic impairment, so consider dose adjustment and titrate with caution, particularly before any increase to 20 mg. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin, troleandomycin) - large rise in lercanidipine levels (up to ~15-fold with ketoconazole); contraindicated
Ciclosporin - mutual increase in plasma levels (lercanidipine ~3-fold); contraindicated
Grapefruit juice - inhibits metabolism and increases hypotensive effect; contraindicated
moderate: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, anticonvulsants such as phenytoin/carbamazepine) - may reduce antihypertensive effect; monitor
Other antihypertensives / diuretics - additive blood-pressure lowering
Simvastatin - lercanidipine increases simvastatin exposure (~56%); take lercanidipine in the morning and simvastatin at night
Midazolam - increased absorption and reduced elimination in the elderly
Beta-blockers (e.g. metoprolol) - reduce lercanidipine bioavailability (~50%); dose adjustment may be needed
minor: Digoxin - small increase in digoxin Cmax (~33%); monitor for toxicity
Cimetidine - higher doses may increase lercanidipine levels
interactions.food: A meal, especially high-fat, increases bioavailability about 4-fold; take at least 15 minutes before food on an empty stomach.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; it may potentiate the vasodilatory and hypotensive effect.
interactions.diagnostics: No clinically important interference with routine laboratory tests reported.

emergency: Anaphylactic reaction / severe angioedema with airway compromise

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate at baseline and during titration
Symptoms of hypotension or worsening angina, especially after initiation or dose increase
Liver function if symptoms suggest hepatic effect
counsel: Take your tablet once a day at least 15 minutes before food, preferably before breakfast
Do not eat grapefruit or drink grapefruit juice while on this medicine
Swelling of the ankles, flushing, or headache may occur early and often settle with time
Do not drink alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much
It may take about 2 weeks to see the full effect; do not stop or change the dose without advice
pk: Gradual; maximal antihypertensive effect develops over about 2 weeks
Plasma Tmax about 1.5-3 hours after dosing
Antihypertensive effect persists ~24 hours due to slow membrane binding
Store in the original packaging to protect from light; below 25 C
pearls: Not FDA-approved; dosing here is taken from EMA/SmPC (UK emc) and the BNF
Take on an empty stomach - food (especially high-fat) increases absorption about 4-fold
High membrane lipophilicity gives a long duration of action despite a short plasma half-life, with little reflex tachycardia
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, ciclosporin, and grapefruit are contraindicated due to large rises in drug levels
Peripheral (ankle) oedema is the typical dose-related dihydropyridine class effect and a common reason for discontinuation
missed: If you miss a dose, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time before food the following day. Do not take two doses together to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause excessive peripheral vasodilation with marked hypotension and reflex tachycardia. Manage with close cardiovascular and respiratory monitoring, elevation of the limbs, attention to circulating fluid volume and urine output; vasopressors and intravenous calcium may be used for severe hypotension/bradycardia. Effects may be prolonged, so monitor for at least 24 hours; dialysis is ineffective because of high protein binding.
